SpaceX is in a different situation. As a completely private entity they report to nobody other than themselves and they plan to test to retropulsive landing on Mars. The idea is simple: land on Mars exactly like they're already landing reusable rockets on Earth - retropulsion. No 1000 mph parachute deployments followed by severing off into a blind freefall and a brief burn followed by a cross your fingers on the crumple zone touchdown. They plan to 'simply' fire their thrusters at supersonic rates and develop autonomous systems to handle all contingencies on the way down where they finally land squarely on 3 legs. And the first time they do it it'll probably set a world record for the biggest explosion on the Martian surface, and that's okay. That's how progress is made and the idea is to learn and adapt. All of their early rocket landing attempts failed but they adjusted from the data and are now regularly landing them - something the old money contractors were saying was impossible just 5 or so years ago.

And once they get this down, it will completely revolutionize our ability to land on Mars. But it starts with removing the assumption that all that matters is short term success. Doing what you know how to do with fear of doing anything else because it might not work is the reason rocket technology today is at best modestly over its state in 1969. How absurd is it that the Saturn V is still a benchmark heavy lift rocket? Improving technology (and really anything complex for that matter) requires an acceptance and even an embracing of failure.
